verses.text: In the twelfth year of Ahaz king of Judah, Hoshea the son of Elah began to reign in Samaria over Israel for nine years.
He did that which was evil in Yahweh’s sight, yet not as the kings of Israel who were before him.
Shalmaneser king of Assyria came up against him, and Hoshea became his servant, and brought him tribute.

The king of Assyria found conspiracy in Hoshea; for he had sent messengers to So king of Egypt, and offered no tribute to the king of Assyria, as he had done year by year. Therefore the king of Assyria seized him, and bound him in prison.
Then the king of Assyria came up throughout all the land, went up to Samaria, and besieged it three years.
In the ninth year of Hoshea the king of Assyria took Samaria, and carried Israel away to Assyria, and placed them in Halah, and on the Habor, the river of Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes.
It was so because the children of Israel had sinned against Yahweh their God, who brought them up out of the land of Egypt from under the hand of Pharaoh king of Egypt, and had feared other gods,
and walked in the statutes of the nations whom Yahweh cast out from before the children of Israel, and of the kings of Israel, which they made.

The children of Israel secretly did things that were not right against Yahweh their God; and they built high places for themselves in all their cities, from the tower of the watchmen to the fortified city;
and they set up for themselves pillars and Asherah poles on every high hill, and under every green tree;
and there they burned incense in all the high places, as the nations whom Yahweh carried away before them did; and they did wicked things to provoke Yahweh to anger;
and they served idols, of which Yahweh had said to them, “You shall not do this thing.”

Yet Yahweh testified to Israel, and to Judah, by every prophet, and every seer, saying, “Turn from your evil ways, and keep my commandments and my statutes, according to all the law which I commanded your fathers, and which I sent to you by my servants the prophets.”
Notwithstanding, they would not listen, but hardened their neck, like the neck of their fathers, who didn’t believe in Yahweh their God.

They rejected his statutes, and his covenant that he made with their fathers, and his testimonies which he testified to them; and they followed vanity, and became vain, and followed the nations that were around them, concerning whom Yahweh had commanded them that they should not do like them.
They abandoned all the commandments of Yahweh their God, and made molten images for themselves, even two calves, and made an Asherah, and worshiped all the army of the sky, and served Baal.
They caused their sons and their daughters to pass through the fire, used divination and enchantments, and sold themselves to do that which was evil in Yahweh’s sight, to provoke him to anger.
Therefore Yahweh was very angry with Israel, and removed them out of his sight. There was none left but the tribe of Judah only.
Also Judah didn’t keep the commandments of Yahweh their God, but walked in the statutes of Israel which they made.
Yahweh rejected all the offspring  of Israel, afflicted them, and delivered them into the hands of raiders, until he had cast them out of his sight.
For he tore Israel from David’s house; and they made Jeroboam the son of Nebat king; and Jeroboam drove Israel from following Yahweh, and made them sin a great sin.
The children of Israel walked in all the sins of Jeroboam which he did; they didn’t depart from them
until Yahweh removed Israel out of his sight, as he said by all his servants the prophets. So Israel was carried away out of their own land to Assyria to this day.

The king of Assyria brought men from Babylon, from Cuthah, from Avva, and from Hamath and Sepharvaim, and placed them in the cities of Samaria instead of the children of Israel; and they possessed Samaria, and lived in its cities.
So it was, at the beginning of their dwelling there, that they didn’t fear Yahweh. Therefore Yahweh sent lions among them, which killed some of them.

Therefore they spoke to the king of Assyria, saying, “The nations which you have carried away and placed in the cities of Samaria don’t know the law of the god of the land. Therefore he has sent lions among them, and behold, they kill them, because they don’t know the law of the god of the land.”
Then the king of Assyria commanded, saying, “Carry there one of the priests whom you brought from there; and let them go and dwell there, and let him teach them the law of the god of the land.”
So one of the priests whom they had carried away from Samaria came and lived in Bethel, and taught them how they should fear Yahweh.
However every nation made gods of their own, and put them in the houses of the high places which the Samaritans had made, every nation in their cities in which they lived.
The men of Babylon made Succoth Benoth, and the men of Cuth made Nergal, and the men of Hamath made Ashima,
and the Avvites made Nibhaz and Tartak; and the Sepharvites burned their children in the fire to Adrammelech and Anammelech, the gods of Sepharvaim.
So they feared Yahweh, and also made from among themselves priests of the high places for themselves, who sacrificed for them in the houses of the high places.
They feared Yahweh, and also served their own gods, after the ways of the nations from among whom they had been carried away.

To this day they do what they did before. They don’t fear Yahweh, and they do not follow the statutes, or the ordinances, or the law, or the commandment which Yahweh commanded the children of Jacob, whom he named Israel;
with whom Yahweh had made a covenant, and commanded them, saying, “You shall not fear other gods, nor bow yourselves to them, nor serve them, nor sacrifice to them;
but you shall fear Yahweh, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt with great power and with an outstretched arm, and you shall bow yourselves to him, and you shall sacrifice to him.
The statutes and the ordinances, and the law and the commandment, which he wrote for you, you shall observe to do forever more. You shall not fear other gods.
You shall not forget the covenant that I have made with you. You shall not fear other gods.
But you shall fear Yahweh your God, and he will deliver you out of the hand of all your enemies.”
However they did not listen, but they did what they did before.
So these nations feared Yahweh, and also served their engraved images. Their children likewise, and their children’s children, as their fathers did, so they do to this day.

footnotes.content: Hoshea takes the throne in the north, while Ahaz reigns in the south. Notice how the kingdoms are now measured against each other—a sign of how far they've drifted from the unity God intended. We mark time by troubled kings.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hoshea did evil, yes, but there's an honest observation here: he was 'not as the kings before him.' We often measure ourselves only against those worse off. But Jesus asks us to measure ourselves against His light, not against the dim lights of those who stumbled before us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Shalmaneser the Assyrian king comes. When we've broken our covenant with God, earthly powers see our weakness. Hoshea pays tribute, thinking he can buy peace. But tribute to an earthly king cannot repair the fracture in our bond with the Almighty.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hoshea seeks Egypt's help—another king, another refuge—but his conspiracy is discovered. How often we play both sides when we should be seeking only one: the Lord. Betrayal catches up; the king locks him away, helpless.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Samaria is besieged for three years—a city of the north, the heart of Israel's kingdom. Time moves slowly when you're surrounded and starving. Long suffering often comes not from a single blow but from a prolonged siege of the soul.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The end comes: Israel is carried away to far places—Halah, Gozan, the cities of the Medes. Whole families torn from their land. This is the cost of turning from God made visible, written in exile and dispersion. The people become strangers in strange lands.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here the Spirit of the historian pauses and names the root: they had sinned against the Lord who brought them up from Egypt. They forgot their Redeemer and feared other gods instead. Ingratitude is the soil where all idolatry grows.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They walked in the statutes of the nations—the very peoples God had cast out before them. We often admire the style, the customs, the 'way of life' of those who don't know the Lord. But we cannot take their paths and end up in His house.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They did these things 'secretly.' There's a quiet shame in idolatry—they built high places but perhaps hoped no one would notice, not God, not their neighbors. But secret sin is never hidden from the Lord; it hollows the soul from within.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pillars and Asherah poles on every high hill, under every green tree—idols multiplied, taking up space in the landscape of daily life. When we clutter our worship with other gods, there's no room left for the One who made us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They burned incense as the nations did, provoking the Lord to anger. Imitation of pagan worship was a deliberate choice, repeated, each time widening the breach. The Lord notices when we embrace the ways of those far from Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They served idols despite the clear command: 'You shall not do this thing.' The word came, plain and direct. Yet they chose differently. Every sin is a small act of defiance against words we knew were true.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yet Yahweh testified—by every prophet, every seer. God did not abandon them; He sent messenger after messenger saying, 'Turn.' The testimony of prophets is a gift of grace itself; the Lord gives chance after chance to those who will listen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They hardened their neck, like their fathers who didn't believe. Stubbornness is learned; it's passed down. When one generation refuses the Lord's voice, the next generation inherits both the pattern and the hardness. Only Jesus can soften such a neck.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They rejected statutes, covenant, testimonies—everything solid that God had given—and followed vanity instead. Vanity is empty air; it makes no promises, keeps none. Yet we run toward it because it asks nothing of us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Two calves, idols of their own making, plus worship of the heavenly bodies and Baal. They didn't stick with one false god; they accumulated them. A hungry heart that refuses the true Bread multiplies counterfeit hungers.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They made their own children pass through fire—the ancient horror of Molech worship. Idolatry demands ever greater sacrifices; it leads parents to betray the ones they should protect most. The pit of false worship has no bottom.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Therefore Yahweh was very angry and removed Israel from His sight. This is the judgment that follows covenant-breaking: separation from the Face of God. Only Judah remains, clinging to the house of David—a remnant held by thread and grace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yet Judah too walked in the statutes Israel made—they watched their northern brothers fall and still imitated them. Sometimes the closest examples are the most dangerous warnings we refuse to heed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh rejected the offspring of Israel, afflicted them, delivered them to raiders. The word 'rejected' cuts deep—yet it is not final. God's rejection of unfaithfulness is not the same as His rejection of His people when they return to Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He tore Israel from David's house when they made Jeroboam king. Jeroboam set up golden calves at Bethel and Dan—the rupture came from a political choice that became a spiritual one. When a leader turns from God, the people follow him into darkness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They walked in all the sins of Jeroboam and didn't depart from them. The first sin becomes a path well-worn; each generation travels it more easily than the one before. Breaking free requires that someone stop and turn back.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Until Yahweh removed Israel—to Assyria, where they stayed, scattered. The prophets had spoken; their warnings stood. When the Lord removes a people from their land, it's not random or accidental; it's the measured consequence of breaking faith with Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king of Assyria brings settlers from Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath, Sepharvaim—a deliberate policy of transplantation. Foreign peoples are planted in Samaria, where Israel once lived. The land is emptied of its people and refilled with strangers.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: These new settlers didn't fear Yahweh, so lions came among them. The land itself, under God's hand, rejects those who have no reverence for Him. Nature is not neutral; it knows its Master.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The settlers speak to the king, saying these lands belong to a god who must be feared. They perceive, without faith, that there is Power here they don't understand. Fear without faith leads them to seek the mechanics of appeasement.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king orders that a priest be sent to teach them the law of the god of the land. A pagan king, managing the land mechanically, arranges for instruction in the God he doesn't know—as if religion were simply technique to master.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A priest from Samaria comes to Bethel and teaches fear of Yahweh. Even in exile, the word goes out; God's truth is not bound to a place or fully silenced. Yet teaching fear is not the same as transforming the heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Every nation made gods of their own. They heard the name of Yahweh but kept their idols too. Syncretism—blending—allows people to think they're obeying while serving themselves. The human heart loves to have it both ways.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Each group brought its gods: Babylon made Succoth Benoth, Cuth made Nergal, Hamath made Ashima. Named gods, each known to its people, each worshiped. The land becomes a pantheon of strange powers.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Sepharvites burned their children to Adrammelech and Anammelech. The horror returns—another people, far from home, continuing to sacrifice their own as their gods demanded. Displacement doesn't stop the worst in us; it often intensifies it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They feared Yahweh and made priests from among themselves for the high places. A folk religion, mixing and blending—they want the benefit of Yahweh's power without the cost of His exclusivity. This is every human heart's bargain with the sacred.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They feared Yahweh and also served their own gods. The contradiction is clear and tragic. We cannot have two masters; one will always rival the other. A heart divided against itself cannot stand whole before God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: To this day, they do what they did before—readers today hear an echo in these words. How often do we find ourselves circling back to old patterns, old gods, old compromises? The Lord offers newness; we reach for the familiar.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh commanded Jacob: fear no other gods. The command is singular, clear, shaped by His covenant love. Yet people will always seek permission to worship multiple lords, as if variety were virtue.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Fear Yahweh, who brought you up from Egypt with great power and an outstretched arm. Every command rests on memory: remember who saved you, who claimed you, who stretched out His arm for your life. We forget the kindness and grow strange to the kind One.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Keep the law forever; fear no other gods. 'Forever' is a long time—longer than kingdoms, longer than exile. God's word stands when earthly powers crumble. A law that lasts forever is not given in anger but in love.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Don't forget the covenant. The word 'forget' stings—God speaks as one who fears being abandoned, left behind. Yet He is never truly forgotten by those who belong to Him; we are written on His hands.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Fear Yahweh your God and He will deliver you from all enemies. The promise is clear: faithfulness brings protection, belonging brings deliverance. But the people turned away from this shelter and chose exposure instead.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: However they did not listen; they did what they did before. Even with the word of God sitting among them, taught by a priest, the people refused. Sometimes the loudest voice in our hearts is our own stubbornness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: These nations feared Yahweh and served their graven images—to this day, the same pattern repeating. A divided heart passes the division down through generations. Only Jesus can break the cycle and teach us to fear the Lord alone with whole and undivided hearts.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
